raw_response:
I've been farming these 10.9 mu for 40 years now, since I was 18. My father taught me, and I've learned a few more things myself over the decades. I'm 58 now — my back isn't what it used to be, and my eyes aren't as good for spotting weeds — but I know every corner of this land. I've got middle school education, so I can read the extension pamphlets the county sends around, but honestly? I trust what I've seen with my own eyes more than what some young agronomist writes on paper.

My household has six people. Two of my children work off-farm in Handan, so they send some money back, but we still depend on this farm for our food and a good part of our income. That means I can't afford big gambles. I play it safe.

I split my land two ways. The better 6.5 mu near the well I keep in the wheat-maize double crop — that's my food security and steady income. The other 4.4 mu I plant cotton. Cotton is more work and more risk, but when the price is decent, it pays better than maize. I've done this mix for years.

**Winter wheat (6.5 mu):** I plant around October 8th to 12th, right after the maize comes off. Last year I got about 450 kg per mu, and the year before about 430. The extension agent says 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is the right amount, but I've always done a bit more — I figure about 17 kg N per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I put down a base of compound fertilizer before planting, about 40 kg per mu, and then at jointing time in March, if the wheat looks a little yellow, I topdress with another 15 kg of urea per mu. I irrigate four times: once before planting if the soil is dry, once in winter if there's no snow, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water costs money — the well is metered now — but a drought year hurts worse than the pumping bill. My neighbor Lao Wang tried cutting back to three irrigations last year and his yield dropped badly, so I'm sticking with four. I use an improved wheat variety I've saved seed from, but I buy fresh seed every few years to keep vigor. This year I'm buying fresh seed — about 35 yuan per mu. For labor, my wife and I do most of it, but at harvest in early June I hire three days of help because the window is tight and I need to get the maize in.

**Summer maize (6.5 mu):** Right after wheat harvest, usually June 12th to 15th, I plant the maize. The turnaround is brutal — sometimes only five or six days. If I can get a custom planter, I hire it. If not, I work from dawn to dark. I plant a hybrid variety; the seed is more expensive, about 50 yuan per mu, but it gives me 500 kg per mu when things go well. I put down about 16 kg N per mu total, split between base and one topdress at the big flare stage. Maize in summer gets some rain, so I only irrigate twice — usually at flowering and if there's a dry spell in August. I spray herbicide once and watch for aphids; if they show up, I spray insecticide. Harvest is late September, and then I immediately till and prepare for wheat again.

**Cotton (4.4 mu):** I plant cotton around April 20th to 25th. It's on the western plot, a bit sandier. Cotton needs a lot of labor — plowing in spring, planting, thinning, watering, spraying, and then picking in multiple rounds from September through October. I put about 14 kg N per mu, with base fertilizer and a topdress at flowering. I irrigate twice, at flowering and boll stage. Pesticides are a must for cotton — bollworm is the big enemy, so I spray insecticide two or three times, plus herbicide and sometimes fungicide if it gets too humid. The picking is what kills me — it's all hand labor. My wife and I do what we can, but I have to hire pickers. That's my biggest cash outlay for cotton, maybe 10 to 12 days of hired labor. I expect about 250 kg of lint per mu if the weather cooperates.

**Why I'm not changing much this year:** Fertilizer prices went up again, and I thought about cutting back, but I remember 2019 when I tried using less and my wheat yield dropped to 380 kg per mu. That loss hurt more than the extra fertilizer cost. So I'll stick with my usual amounts. I also thought about switching the cotton plot to wheat-maize to reduce labor — I'm not getting younger — but cotton prices look decent this year, and I need the cash income. My children send money, but I don't want to depend on that for every little thing.

Total input costs will run me about 7,400 yuan for the year. That's a big chunk of cash to lay out, but I've been saving since the summer maize sale. I keep a reserve. Always keep a reserve.
